sections.h: Zechariah 1-8: the dated half of the book
sections.b: Chapters 1-8 are dated to the second and fourth years of Darius I (520-518 BC). They open with a call to turn back (1:1-6), then eight visions in one night, 15 February 519 (1:7-6:8), then a crowning (6:9-15) and an answer to a question about fasting (7:1-8:23). The community is the small province of Judah under Zerubbabel and Joshua, building the Temple that was finished in March 515. Haggai is its partner (Ezra 5:1; Ezra 6:14). The Hebrew and English numbers differ only at 1:18-21 (Hebrew 2:1-4).
sections.refs: Zechariah 1:1-6; Zechariah 1:7-6:15; Zechariah 7:1-8:23; Ezra 5:1-2; Ezra 6:14-15; Haggai 1:1

sections.h: Four themes of the first half
sections.b: The first half returns to four themes. The LORD returns to Jerusalem and comforts it (1:13-17; 8:3). The Temple will be finished by the LORD's Spirit, through Zerubbabel's hands (4:6-9). The community is called to turn back and to live in justice and truth (1:3-6; 7:9-10; 8:16-17). The nations will join the LORD in Jerusalem (2:11; 8:20-23). The call to turn back at 1:3 and the fasting answer at 8:19 frame the whole.
sections.refs: Zechariah 1:3; Zechariah 2:11; Zechariah 4:6-9; Zechariah 7:9-10; Zechariah 8:3; Zechariah 8:16-23

sections.h: The eight visions of one night
sections.b: The visions run from 1:8 to 6:8, on the night of 15 February 519 BC. They are the horsemen among the myrtle trees (1:8-17), the four horns and four craftsmen (1:18-21), the man with the measuring cord (2:1-5), Joshua and the Accuser (3:1-10), the lampstand and the two olive trees (4:1-14), the flying scroll (5:1-4), the woman in the ephah (5:5-11) and the four chariots (6:1-8). In each the prophet sees, asks "What is this?" and is answered by "the angel who spoke with me." Horses open the series and chariots close it, and the LORD's spirit comes to rest in the north (6:8). Some scholars count seven by joining the two scenes of chapter 5.
sections.refs: Zechariah 1:7-6:8; Ezekiel 40:1-4; Daniel 7:1-28; Daniel 8:1-27; Amos 7:1-9; Amos 8:1-3

sections.h: The vision of Wickedness in a basket
sections.b: In the seventh of the night visions, a woman called Wickedness sits inside an ephah, a grain-measuring basket, under a lead lid. Two winged women carry it between earth and sky to the land of Shinar, to build it a house. Readers have taken the woman as a goddess sent back to Babylon, as the land's sin sent away, or as the dishonest commerce symbolized by the false ephah. The vision comes just after the flying scroll's curse on thieves and false swearers (5:1-4).

sections.h: "Not by strength and not by force, but by my Spirit"
sections.b: The line is spoken to Zerubbabel about the Temple (Zechariah 4:6). It says that the work will rise by the LORD's Spirit and not by army or force; the next verses give Zerubbabel's hands the job of laying the foundation and finishing it (4:9). It is often used as a motto for trusting God. The first setting is narrower: a Davidic governor in a Persian province, a few years after revolts that might have drawn Jewish hopes.

sections.h: The fasts of the fourth, fifth, seventh and tenth months
sections.b: Four fasts kept the memory of 586 BC: the tenth month for the start of the siege (2 Kings 25:1), the fourth for the breach of the wall (Jeremiah 39:2), the fifth for the burning of the Temple (2 Kings 25:8-9) and the seventh for the murder of Gedaliah (2 Kings 25:25; Jeremiah 41:1-3). Zechariah 7:3-5 asks whether the fasts of the fifth and seventh months were for the LORD, and 8:19 promises that all four will become joy and gladness and good feasts. Jewish practice still keeps 10 Tevet, 17 Tammuz, 9 Av and 3 Tishri; the Talmud (Rosh Hashanah 18b) discusses when they bind.
sections.refs: Zechariah 7:1-7; Zechariah 8:18-19; 2 Kings 25:1; 2 Kings 25:8-9; 2 Kings 25:25; Jeremiah 39:2; Jeremiah 41:1-3; Jeremiah 52:4-7

sections.h: The measuring line for destruction and for building
sections.b: A line stretched over a city can mark it for destruction (2 Kings 21:13; Isaiah 34:11; Lamentations 2:8) or for building (Jeremiah 31:38-40; Ezekiel 40:3; Zechariah 1:16; Zechariah 2:1-2). In Zechariah the line becomes a promise (1:16), and then a man goes to measure Jerusalem, only to learn that the city will outgrow any wall (2:1-5). In Revelation a rod is given to measure the temple (Revelation 11:1) and an angel measures the new Jerusalem (Revelation 21:15).
sections.refs: Zechariah 1:16; Zechariah 2:1-5; 2 Kings 21:13; Isaiah 34:11; Lamentations 2:8; Jeremiah 31:38-40; Ezekiel 40:3; Revelation 11:1; Revelation 21:15

sections.b: Yehud was the Persian name for the province of Judah, a small district in the satrapy "Beyond the River." Its governors included Zerubbabel (Haggai 1:1) and later Nehemiah. In Zechariah's day it was a poor district around Jerusalem with a few thousand people. Zechariah looks back to the larger kingdom with its Negev and Shephelah (7:7) and forward to a Jerusalem too full for walls (2:4).

Zechariah names the Branch twice: "my servant, the Branch" whom the LORD is about to bring (3:8), and "a man whose name is Branch" who "will branch out" from his own place and build the LORD's temple, bear majesty, sit and rule on his throne, and be a priest on his throne (6:12-13). The Greek writes "Anatolē," dawn or rising, which Luke 1:78 can echo. The Branch may be Zerubbabel, the Davidic governor and builder (Haggai 2:23; Zechariah 4:9), or a king still to come, or both; the Targum reads "the Messiah."
sections.refs: Zechariah 3:8; Zechariah 6:12-13; Haggai 2:23; Zechariah 4:9; Jeremiah 23:5; Jeremiah 33:15; Luke 1:78

common: The Branch (tsemach) is a name for the Davidic king. In Zechariah it has been read as Zerubbabel (many critical scholars), as the Messiah (the Targum, "my servant the Messiah," at 3:8 and 6:12), as Christ (Christian reading, with the Greek Anatole behind Luke 1:78), and as both a sign for Zerubbabel's day and a hope still to come.
uncommon: The crowning in 6:11 once named Zerubbabel and was changed to Joshua (Mitchell, Rudolph and others).

sections.b: In Zechariah 3:1-2 "the Accuser" stands at the right hand of Joshua the high priest in the court of the angel of the LORD, "to accuse him," and the LORD rebukes him. As in Job 1-2 the word has the article and is a title, an officer who charges. He acts as a prosecutor in a trial, not as a ruler of evil. The Greek has diabolos. Jude 9 quotes the rebuke, and Revelation 12:10 names the devil "the accuser of our brothers."
sections.refs: Zechariah 3:1-2; Job 1:6-12; Job 2:1-7; 1 Chronicles 21:1; Psalm 109:6; Jude 9; Revelation 12:10

common: Most critical commentators: in Zechariah 3 and Job 1-2 the Accuser is an officer of God's court, not yet the devil of the New Testament.
Christian tradition from the Fathers on: the Accuser is the devil (the Greek has diabolos; Revelation 12:10 names the devil "the accuser of our brothers").
Jewish tradition: a prosecuting angel in the heavenly court who serves God's purposes.

sections.h: Joshua in Zechariah's vision and crowning
sections.b: Zechariah 3 shows Joshua standing in filthy clothes before the angel of the LORD, accused by the Accuser, then cleansed, robed and given a clean turban and a charge to walk in the LORD's ways, keep his duty, govern the house and guard the courts (3:1-7). In 6:9-15 he is crowned with silver and gold crowns made from a gift from the exiles. The Greek calls him Iēsous, and Justin Martyr read the scene as Jesus Christ and his people (Dialogue 115-116).

Zechariah promises Zerubbabel that the great mountain will become a plain and that his hands, which laid the foundation, will finish the Temple (4:6-10). The word that opens the oracle, "Not by strength and not by force, but by my Spirit," is the book's best-known line. Zerubbabel may be the Branch (3:8; 6:12), and he is one of the "sons of fresh oil" (4:14). He is not named in 6:9-15, and the book does not say what became of him.

sections.h: The Branch and the two sons of fresh oil
sections.b: In Zechariah 1-8 the royal hope is attached to Zerubbabel and the priestly hope to Joshua. The book calls them the "two sons of fresh oil" (4:14) and speaks of a coming Branch who will sit on a throne with a priest at his side or on it (6:13). The Targum reads the Branch as the Messiah, and the Qumran community later expected two Messiahs (in its Community Rule). Christians read the Branch of Zechariah as Christ, the priest-king.

sections.h: Zechariah and the building of the Temple
sections.b: Zechariah worked beside Haggai on the Temple. His visions promise that the LORD will return to Jerusalem and his house be rebuilt (1:16), that the house Zerubbabel founded his hands will bring to completion (4:9), that the prophet's word will be proved when it stands finished (4:9), and that people from far away will help to build (6:15). The Temple was finished on 12 March 515 BC (Ezra 6:15). Chapters 7-8 deal with the fasts that mourned its loss.
sections.refs: Zechariah 1:16; Zechariah 4:9; Zechariah 6:12-15; Zechariah 8:9; Ezra 5:1-2; Ezra 6:14-15

sections.b: Zechariah's dates are by the reign of Darius I (1:1, 7; 7:1), and the first vision finds the earth "settled and quiet" after the revolts of 522-521 (1:11). The image of riders walking the earth recalls the Persian courier and inspection system, and the seven eyes of the LORD recall the king's eyes. The book does not name Persia; its enemy is Babylon, and the horns scattered Judah, Israel and Jerusalem (1:19). Persia's own policy is the background of the Temple's permission (Ezra 6).

A delegation asks whether the fast of the fifth month should go on now the Temple is being rebuilt (7:3). The LORD asks back: "Did you really fast for me, for me?" (7:5), and calls the people to justice and care for the poor (7:9-10). Then he promises that the four fasts will become joy and gladness and good feasts (8:19). The prophets' tests for a fast are in Isaiah 58:3-7 and Joel 2:12-13.

The Spirit appears in three places in Zechariah 1-8. At 4:6 the Temple will be built "not by strength and not by force, but by my Spirit." At 6:8 the LORD's "spirit" (anger or Spirit) is set at rest in the north. At 7:12 the earlier prophets' words were sent "by his Spirit." Haggai had said the same: "my spirit is standing among you" (Haggai 2:5).

sections.h: The angel who spoke with me
sections.b: The interpreting angel of Zechariah appears in every vision of 1:8-6:8 as "the angel who spoke with me." He explains the vision, sends another angel with a message (2:3-4) and calls to the prophet (6:8). Other angels include the angel of the LORD at the myrtles (1:11-12), the two winged women of 5:9, and the four winds or spirits of 6:5. The pattern of seer and interpreting angel runs through Ezekiel, Daniel and Revelation.
sections.refs: Zechariah 1:9; Zechariah 2:3; Zechariah 5:5; Zechariah 6:5; Ezekiel 40:3; Daniel 8:16; Revelation 17:1

sections.h: The angel of the LORD in Zechariah
sections.b: In 1:11-12 the angel of the LORD stands among the myrtle trees, receives the riders' report and pleads for Jerusalem. In 3:1-6 he presides at Joshua's trial and speaks the pardon. He is distinct from the LORD, who answers him with comforting words (1:13) and who rebukes the Accuser. Jewish readers take him as an angel; many Christian writers have taken him as the Son before his birth.

sections.h: The lampstand and the two olive trees
sections.b: Zechariah's lampstand is all of gold, with a bowl, seven lamps and pipes, fed by two olive trees on either side (4:2-3, 11-12). The seven lamps are the seven eyes of the LORD (4:10), and the olive trees are "the two sons of fresh oil who stand by the Lord of the whole earth" (4:14). In Revelation the seven lampstands are the churches (Revelation 1:20) and "the two olive trees and the two lampstands" are the two witnesses (Revelation 11:4).

The LORD says he has come back to Jerusalem with compassion (1:16), will make his home in the middle of it (2:10; 8:3), and will be a wall of fire around it and its glory inside (2:5). The city will be called the City of Truth (8:3); old and young will fill its squares (8:4-5). The nations will come to seek the LORD there (8:20-23). A man measures it (2:1-2), and the angel says it will be too full for walls (2:4).

Zechariah 2:7 speaks of Zion "who live with Daughter Babylon," the exiles living in Babylon, and 2:10 summons Daughter Zion to shout for joy because the LORD is coming. The two cities stand as two women, one to be left and one to be gladdened. The summons of 2:10 is close to Zephaniah 3:14-17 and is the text for the first Sabbath of Hanukkah (Hebrew 2:14).

The "land of the north" is Babylon (2:6; 6:6, 8), and the exiles are told to flee it (2:6-7). The black chariot team goes to the north and "quiets my spirit" there (6:8). A delegation of exiles brings silver and gold from Babylon (6:10). The ephah with Wickedness goes to Shinar, the old name for Babylonia (5:11). Revelation 18:4 uses the call of 2:6-7 against a later Babylon.

The exile is the background to the book: seventy years of indignation (1:12), a scattering by four horns (1:19), a call to those still in Babylon (2:6-7), and a delegation of exiles bringing gifts (6:10). Zechariah 8:7 promises the LORD will save his people "from the land of the east and from the land of the setting sun." The fasts of 7:3-5 and 8:19 keep the memory of 586.
sections.refs: Zechariah 1:12; Zechariah 1:19; Zechariah 2:6-7; Zechariah 6:10; Zechariah 7:5; Zechariah 8:7

sections.b: Zechariah mentions the seventy years twice: the angel asks how long the LORD will be indignant with Jerusalem "these seventy years" (1:12), and the LORD asks the people about fasts "these seventy years" (7:5). Counted from 586, the span ends about 519-518, the dates of the two messages.

Zechariah uses "the remnant of this people" three times in chapter 8 (verses 6, 11, 12) and calls Joshua "a piece of firewood snatched from the fire" (3:2), as Amos 4:11 calls Israel. The remnant is the community under Zerubbabel and Joshua (Haggai 1:12-14). The LORD says he will not treat them as in the former days (8:11) and will give them the harvest as an inheritance (8:12).

sections.h: The covenant formula and the curse in Zechariah
sections.b: Zechariah uses the covenant formula "they will be my people, and I will be their God" (8:8) and applies it to the nations (2:11). The flying scroll carries the covenant's curse against theft and false oaths (5:1-4), and the book's last promise of 6:15 depends on obeying the LORD's voice. 1:3-6 and 7:11-14 recall the curses that overtook the ancestors.
sections.refs: Zechariah 2:11; Zechariah 5:1-4; Zechariah 6:15; Zechariah 8:8; Deuteronomy 28; Deuteronomy 29:19-21

sections.b: The earlier prophets' message, which the ancestors refused, was "Judge with true justice. Show loyal love and compassion, each to his brother. Do not oppress the widow or the fatherless, the foreigner who lives among you or the poor. And do not plan harm against one another in your hearts" (Zechariah 7:9-10). The same commands return at 8:16-17: speak the truth, judge with truth and justice that makes for peace, plan no harm, love no false oath. Paul quotes 8:16 in Ephesians 4:25.

sections.h: The foreigner who lives among you
sections.b: Zechariah 7:10 lists the foreigner who lives among you (ger) with the widow, the fatherless and the poor, those the law protects. Later the nations themselves join the LORD (2:11) and come to Jerusalem (8:20-23), and ten men from every language hold on to the robe of a Jew (8:23).

Zechariah's visions show a heavenly court: the riders who report to the angel of the LORD (1:10-11), the Accuser at the right hand of the accused (3:1), the attendants who remove the filthy clothes (3:4) and "these who stand here," among whom Joshua is promised a place (3:7). The four winds or spirits present themselves before the Lord of the whole earth (6:5), as the sons of God do in Job 1:6.

sections.h: Filth, flint and a house to tear down
sections.b: Zechariah has Joshua in clothes named for filth (3:3-4) and a curse that destroys a house "timbers and stones" (5:4), like the house with spreading mold that must be torn down in Leviticus 14:45. A woman called Wickedness is sealed in a measure and carried off on the wings of unclean storks (5:7-9; Leviticus 11:19).

Zechariah gives the high priest a charge: walk in the LORD's ways, carry out his assigned duty, govern the house and guard its courtyards (3:7). He is given a clean turban (3:5) and in 6:11 crowned. The priest sits with a Branch on a throne and a plan of peace is between the two (6:13). After the exile the high priest became the main leader of the community.

sections.h: The crowned priest and the Branch king
sections.b: In 6:11 crowns are made for Joshua the high priest, and in 6:12-13 a Branch sits and rules on his throne. The usual Hebrew word for a royal crown is used ('atarah). Zerubbabel the Davidic governor does not wear a crown in the book. The relation between priest and king is a plan of peace "between the two of them."

The LORD promises Jerusalem a wall of fire around it and himself as the glory inside it (2:5). The glory that had left the Temple in Ezekiel (Ezekiel 10:18-19; 11:22-23) returns to the new house (Ezekiel 43:1-5), and Haggai says the LORD will fill the house with glory (Haggai 2:7, 9). Zechariah's own words are the LORD's presence in Zion (2:10; 8:3).

sections.h: Nations joining the LORD in Zechariah 1-8
sections.b: Zechariah 2:11 says that "On that day many nations will attach themselves to the LORD, and they will become my people." 6:15 says that "those who are far away will come and build the temple of the LORD." 8:20-23 describes peoples and mighty nations coming to seek the LORD in Jerusalem, and ten men from every language holding the robe of one Jew. How these relate to the church and to Israel is read differently by Jews, Catholics, Reformed, Dispensationalists and Messianic Jews.

The flying scroll is a curse against the thief and the false swearer, entering their houses (5:1-4). The ancestors were a curse among the nations, and will become a blessing (8:13). The drought and poverty of the earlier years (8:10) give way to a sowing in peace, with the vine, the land and the heavens giving their fruit, produce and dew (8:12). Haggai had the same pattern (Haggai 1:10-11; 2:19).

sections.h: "I did not change my mind" in Zechariah 8
sections.b: In 8:14 the LORD says that when the ancestors provoked him he planned harm and "did not change my mind," and in the next verse he has turned again and planned good. The same root appears in 1:13 and 1:17 for comfort. The pattern is that the LORD is not talked out of a judgment that is deserved, and he is not talked out of a mercy he has promised (8:15).
sections.refs: Zechariah 8:14-15; Zechariah 1:6; Zechariah 1:13; Zechariah 1:17; Jeremiah 4:28; Jeremiah 18:8

sections.h: "Return to me, and I will return to you"
sections.b: The first message of Zechariah is a call to return, based on what happened to the ancestors who did not (1:2-6). The LORD's own return to Zion is the second half of the exchange (1:16; 8:3). The prophets' call to justice (7:9-10; 8:16-17) is what return looks like, and the word "if you really listen" ends 6:15. Malachi 3:7 repeats the promise.

Zechariah sends the ephah with the woman Wickedness to "the land of Shinar" to build a house for it (5:11). Shinar is the plain where Nimrod's kingdom began (Genesis 10:10) and where people built the city and tower of Babel (Genesis 11:2). The vision places evil's house in the land of human pride.

Zechariah is the eleventh of the Twelve in the Hebrew order and the eleventh in the Greek order (Hosea, Amos, Micah, Joel, Obadiah, Jonah, Nahum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah, Haggai, Zechariah, Malachi). Chapters 1-8 are dated like Haggai and share its names, dates and terms, so Haggai and Zechariah 1-8 are often read as a pair (Meyers and Meyers; Petersen). The dating formula and the "before the exile" voice of the earlier prophets (1:4; 7:7, 12) tie the book to the whole collection. The call to "return" in 1:3 is answered by Malachi 3:7.

Zechariah is named in his book as "son of Berechiah, son of Iddo" (1:1, 7), in Ezra as "son of Iddo" (Ezra 5:1; Ezra 6:14), and in Nehemiah 12:16 as the head of Iddo's priestly house. His dated messages are 1:1 (late October-November 520 BC), 1:7 (15 February 519) and 7:1 (7 December 518). He speaks within his own visions (3:5; 4:4, 11).
